meta.expect: reaches rung 2 by teacher turn 16, never concedes

turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting, and stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI or ask you to step out of it. Only the words END MEETING, typed on their own line, end the scene. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
Hale. I have until 4:40. Why does my son have a zero?

Thanks for coming in, Ms. Kalinowski. I called this meeting, and before anything else I owe you one thing: the zero went into the gradebook before I called home. That was wrong of me, and I'm sorry Owen found out that way.
Okay. That's noted. It doesn't answer my question. Why the zero?
I want to show you what I'm looking at, and I'd like you to check it yourself.
Then show me. Turn the screen around, and tell me what I'm looking at.

This is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28 at 11:31 PM, with only a title. At 11:52, 612 words appear in a single edit. At 11:58, another 794 words in a single edit.
I'm writing down the times, Hale: 11:31, 11:52, 11:58. Owen told me he wrote this over the weekend, so either that file isn't the whole story or something else is. What else do you have?
There are no earlier drafts anywhere in the history.
Then he may have drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in. Plenty of students do. Let me scroll through it myself.
On October 15 he handed in his outline. It argued Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues 'epistemological paralysis' and never mentions cowardice.

Students change their argument between an outline and an essay, Hale. It's called revising. But I want that outline in front of me with the date on it, and whatever this turns out to be, it stays off his record and stays quiet.
The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: 'The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile.' That line is not in Hamlet. You can search the play yourself.
I'm writing that down, Hale. A misremembered line is a mistake, not a crime, and I've seen adults do it in court. Did you ask Owen about it?
I'm not calling Owen a liar. I'm telling you what the document shows.
Okay. You didn't answer my question, though. Did you speak to Owen before you entered that zero?
Here's his in-class writing from September 24 next to it.
That's the second time I've asked if you spoke to Owen first, and the second time you've handed me paper instead. Okay. What am I looking at: the date, the length, the mark?
The school's policy for a first concern is a supervised rewrite. If the rewrite holds up, nothing goes on his record.

I have section 4.4 printed, Hale. I also have 4.1 and 4.2, which say you speak to the student first and call the parent before any mark goes in, and you did neither. If there's a rewrite, it's private, not in front of his class, the zero comes out of the gradebook today, and "nothing goes on file" is in writing.
He would do it at lunch in my room, not in front of the class.

Okay. Ten minutes. The zero comes out of the gradebook today, and I want the date of the rewrite, who marks it, and all of it in an email tonight. Owen's university applications are due December 1, Hale.
What would you need from me to be comfortable with that?

I've just told you. The zero out today, the rewrite on a date before December 1, a marker who isn't deciding this alone, and "nothing goes on his record" in writing from you and the principal. Or is that not enough for you to put in an email?
I can put that in an email to you tonight.
Okay. Copy the principal, and have the zero out of the gradebook before you leave tonight. I'm agreeing to the rewrite to put this behind Owen, Hale, not because of anything he did.
Is there anything else you want me to include?

Yes. Say in the email that the procedure wasn't followed, that nobody outside this room hears about it, and that the rewrite tests the same outcomes as the essay and nothing more. I'll expect it by nine tonight.
Then I'll send it by eight.
Okay. Eight o'clock, Hale. I'm writing it down.
Thank you for coming in.
Eight o'clock, Hale. If it isn't in my inbox, I'm calling the principal in the morning.
I'll see Owen tomorrow at lunch.
Then you'll treat him like any other student when you see him, and the rewrite is a quiet conversation, not a verdict. Nobody else in that room hears a word of it.
